## Considered and refused

- 1842 `l` “I have not heard” (planned change to “I did not hear”): refused. The prologue’s `ne hȳrde ic cȳmlīcor` (38) has `l` “I have not heard”, and the shared glossary agrees (“ne hȳrde ic ‘I have not heard’”). House practice, not an error.
- 1821 `i` “you have served us well”: refused. Fitt 20 (1343) renders `dohte` “served”, and fitt 08 “availed” in `l`; the pair is house.
- 1885 `l` “which has often harmed many” for masculine `sē þe`: kept. The note states the gender mismatch with `yldo` and the apparatus `sēo`, calls the antecedent a guess, and a literal “he who” would point to the king.
- 1822 `i` “by deeds of war” and `gūðgeweorca`: kept as a flagged guess; no reading of the genitive is better supported, and the note now says what it might hang on.
- 1850 `i` “Geats” for `Sǣ-Gēatas`: kept; same treatment as `Weder-Gēata` → “Geats” in the house table, and `l` has “Sea-Geats”.
- 1860 `l` “shall greet” for the infinitive `gegrēttan`: kept; it is governed by the `sceal` of 1855, which the note now says.
- 1873 whether `Him` is “them” or Hrothgar alone, and which man `ōþres` names: not decidable from the grammar; the draft’s reading is kept, labelled a guess, and sent to the questions entry.
- 1841 `wigtig`: kept as “wise”, a spelling of `wītig` (cf. `wītig Drihten`, 1554); the “war-skilled” alternative stays in the note.
- 1850 `hordweard hæleþa` general or aimed at Beowulf: left open as the draft had it.
- 1836 `geþingeð`: no firmer lemma available from the sole-source aids; the sense “resorts” stays a flagged guess.
- 1826 `ofer flōda begang` with `gefricge` rather than with `þȳwað`: chosen by sense (`i` agrees now); the other attachment is not argued in the note.
- 1817, 1840 notes: “gives the king’s reply the same weight …” is a mild closer but states what the formula does; left.
- Notes over 150 words (1822, 1826, 1830, 1836, 1845, 1850, 1855, 1870, 1873, 1878, 1885): the validator will WARN, not fail; the published parts carry such notes; splitting them would lose the apparatus detail. Left for the owner.
- `p` flags (1817, 1840, 1866 only): unchanged; 1884 could start a paragraph where the poet turns to praise Hrothgar, but nothing in the conventions requires it.
- Dot under a vowel: none occurs in lines 1817–1887, so no explanation is owed. The low-confidence circumflex at 1883 is reported in the note and kept.
- Packet check: all seven italic letters (1833, 1836, 1857, 1862, 1868, 1880) and every bracket/parenthesis ([h]ine, h[ī]e, seoðða(n), [nō], ðegn[a], āge[n]dfreân) are explained in a note; none missing.
- Source check: the units’ `t` joined equal lines 1817–1887 of the source (whitespace-normalised); `t`, `ln`, `v`, `p` identical to the draft, checked by script before every write.
- `gloss.json` is not yet written, so the planned second-pass gloss check could not be done here. For the glosser: `bēo` (1825) is 1st singular present, not imperative; `gesōhte` (1839) and `geworhte` (1864) are plural participles; `ealdor` (1848) is accusative; `ealde wīsan` (1865) accusative; `blōde` after `wið` (1880) is not instrumental “with blood”; `egesan` (1827) dative or accusative; `ðe` (1846) the particle.

Pass 1 H/M/L 1/24/16, pass 2 H/M/L 1/6/12.

## Gloss check

Checked every novel entry (80) and every `__broaden__` entry (28) of `gloss.json` against its line(s), the grammar and the shared glossary (each broadened entry starts with the shared glossary's old entry whole, then ` · `; verified by script), and went through all 212 known forms for uses their existing entry does not cover. Every token of lines 1817–1887 is in `novel-forms.json` or `known-forms.json`; the novel keys equal the `gloss.json` keys. Edits were made by script; the file is still valid JSON in the same shape.

| Form | Sev. | Wrong | Done |
|---|---|---|---|
| dryhten | M | Broadening gave only the vocative (1824); the use in apposition to the dative `Higelāce` (`Gēata dryhten`, 1831, where the apparatus has editors printing `dryhtne`) was uncovered. | Third reading added: nominative form in apposition to a dative; case does not agree. |
| hyrde | M | Existing entry covers nominative and accusative; `folces hyrde` at 1832 stands beside the dative `Higelāce`. | Broadened: apposition to a dative; same form in nominative, accusative, dative. |
| bringan | M | “strong verb”: `bringan` is an irregular weak verb (preterite `brōhte`). | Class corrected. |
| gegrēttan | M | “here with gōdum”: breaks the rule against “here”. | Reworded (“with the dative of the gift, as in gōdum”). |
| sŷ | L | Lemma `bēon`; the shared glossary files `sīe` under `wesan`, and `sŷ` is the same subjunctive. | Lemma `wesan`, `sŷ` a variant of `sīe`. |
| þǣm | L | Existing entry has no dative singular masculine as antecedent of a relative (`þǣm þe him selfa dēah`, 1839). | Broadened. |
| hetende | L | “present participle of hatian”: the i-umlaut points to `hettan` (the apparatus prints `hettende`). | Derivation given as `hettan`, cf. `hete`. |
| wigtig | L | “the manuscript form”: the packet does not say what the manuscript has. | “printed form”, with the `wīg` reading named as the alternative. |
| gefricge, herige | L | Called plainly subjunctive; the 1st singular present has one form for both moods. `gefricge` also derived from `frignan` (class III) while the class V verb is `fricgan`. | Mood stated with the caveat; `fricgan` named. |
| dohtest | L | Example “you were of good to us” is not English. | “you were of use to us”. |
| bewenede, willum | L | “indulged in (our) wishes” suggests a preposition; `willum` is a dative of means. | “indulged with …”. |
| blondenfeaxum | L | “of the old king” pins the entry to the line; dative plural not mentioned. | Pin removed; “same form serves the dative plural”. |

Checked and kept: all other novel parses (case, number, gender, tense, mood, lemma) agree with the lines. All other `__broaden__` additions are correct for their lines: `andsware` (dative), `blōde` (dative after `wið`), `bād`, `bēo` (1st singular present), `cyning` (accusative), `dyrne`, `ealdor` (accusative), `ealdum` (dative singular, as the unit reads it), `egesan`, `fremman`, `geongum`, `gesōhte`, `geworhte` (participle), `guman`, `Higelāc` (accusative), `hordweard`, `swǣse`, `tō` (`tō þon`), `wīdan`, `wīsan`, `wǣron` (1st plural), `ðe` (particle, 1846 included), `ðē`, `þingian`, `þīn`, `þīnre`, `sēlran`. Known forms with an existing entry that covers their use here were left alone.

Refused:
- `māran` (1823): the existing entry (accusative singular masculine, used as a noun) matches the unit's chosen reading; the alternative (agreeing with `mōdlufan`) is already flagged as the other possibility in the note, so no broadening.
- `mōston` (1875): the existing entry says preterite subjunctive although `-on` is the indicative plural ending (subjunctive would be `mōsten`). An existing entry may not be rewritten, and the meaning is right; recorded here only.
- `gange` (1884), `geþingeð` (1837), `geæhted` (1884): glosses are hedged as guesses and match the unit notes; no better-supported reading in the public-domain aids.
- `heorugrimme` (1847): the final `-e` is unusual for a strong feminine nominative; no source consulted settles it, so the entry stands unchanged.

Gloss check H/M/L 0/4/8.
